title: Classes and objects in C++ — practice
subject: computer-science

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a class and an object?

choices.text: A class is a plan; an object is one thing made from that plan, with its own values
A class is one thing; an object is the plan for many things
They are two words for the same thing
A class holds only data and an object holds only functions

questions.explanation: A class is like the plan of a house, and objects are the houses built from it. From one `Student` class you can make many students, each with its own name and mark.

questions.prompt: Which line creates an object `s` of the class `Student` with its default constructor?

choices.text: `Student s;`
`Student s();`
`Student.s;`
`s = Student;`

questions.explanation: Write the class name, then the object name, as for a variable: `Student s;`. With empty brackets, `Student s();` is read by C++ as the declaration of a function called `s`, not as an object.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true about a constructor? Select **all** that apply.

choices.text: It has the same name as the class
It runs automatically when an object is created
It has no return type, not even `void`
A class can have only one constructor
You must call it yourself after creating the object

questions.explanation: A constructor has the class's name and no return type, and C++ calls it by itself when the object is created. A class can have several constructors with different parameters, such as `Student()` and `Student(string n, int m)`.

questions.prompt: In a C++ `class`, members are `public` until you write `private:`.
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: in a `class`, members are `private` until you write `public:`. In a `struct`, they are `public` by default.

Each object has its own `value`, and both start at 0. For `a`: 5 is added, −2 is ignored because it is not positive, and 4 is added, so `a.get()` is 9. For `b`: 3 is added, so `b.get()` is 3. The program prints $9 + 3 = 12$.

questions.prompt: In `main()`, the line `acc.balance = 500;` does not compile, but `acc.deposit(500);` does. Why?

choices.text: `balance` is private, so only the methods of the class can use it
`balance` has not been given a value yet
The dot operator only works with methods
500 is too big for an `int`

questions.explanation: This is **encapsulation**: the data is private, and other code changes it only through public methods such as `deposit()`, which check each amount.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the idea of keeping an object's data private and changing it only through public methods?
questions.explanation: **Encapsulation** protects the data: a bank account's balance can only change through `deposit()` and `withdraw()`, which check the rules.

questions.prompt: In a class diagram, which line shows a **private** attribute `fuel` of type `double`?

choices.text: `- fuel : double`
`+ fuel : double`
`- fuel() : double`
`double : fuel -`

questions.explanation: A minus sign means private and a plus sign means public. Attributes have no brackets; methods do, as in `+ getFuel() : double`.

questions.prompt: Write a C++ class `Phone` with two private attributes, `owner` (a `string`) and `battery` (an `int`, in percent). Give it a constructor that sets both attributes, a public method `charge(int amount)` that adds a positive amount but never lets the battery go above 100, and a getter `getBattery()`. Then write a `main()` that creates Keza's phone at 40% and charges it by 30.
questions.explanation: A good answer keeps `owner` and `battery` private, sets them in a constructor `Phone(string o, int b)`, and only changes the battery in `charge()`, which adds positive amounts and stops at 100. `Phone p("Keza", 40); p.charge(30);` then gives a battery of 70%, and a second `p.charge(50);` would give 100%, not 120%.
